Isle
īle
n. (an island or coastland; in the prophets, the far nations awaiting the Messiah; rendering Hebrew i, plural iyyim)
From Latin insula through Old French. The Hebrew i means a coastland or habitable shore, and in Isaiah it becomes shorthand for the ends of the earth.

Biblical Definition

Isle in the Authorized Version usually means a coastland, and in the prophets it is a missionary word. The table of nations begins it: “By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue” (Gen 10:5) — the nations scattered at Babel, filed under the isles. Isaiah then makes them the object of the Servant's work: “He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4) — a promise quoted over Christ in Matthew 12, and one that no reading confined to Israel can contain. The Psalter joins the summons: “The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1). And Isaiah 24:15 calls for His name to be glorified “in the isles of the sea”. To the Hebrew ear the isles were the outermost places, past the last trade route — and they are precisely where the prophets expect the gospel to arrive.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water, or a detached portion of land embosomed in the ocean — noting that in Scripture it often denotes a maritime country or coast.

ISLE, n. ile. A tract of land surrounded by water; an island.

In Scripture, isle sometimes denotes a country not connected with any known continent, or one distant from Judea.

The isles shall wait for his law. Is. xlii.

2. A passage in a church or cathedral; more properly aisle.

Key Scripture

Isa 42:4 — "He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law."

Gen 10:5 — "By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations."

Psa 97:1 — "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof."

Isa 24:15 — "Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea."

Modern Corruption

The Great Commission narrowed to what is near and comfortable, while the prophets set the Servant's reach at the isles — the last places on the map, waiting for His law.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure is one of horizon. Isaiah 42:4 does not present the isles as an optional extension of the Servant's work but as its measure: He will not fail nor be discouraged till He has set judgment in the earth, and the isles wait for His law. A church whose vision ends at its own coastline has a smaller Christ than Isaiah's, and the correction is not guilt but expectation. The isles are waiting; the outcome is not in doubt.

Genesis 10:5 supplies the historical frame that makes the promise sweet. The isles of the Gentiles are the scattering of Babel, divided by tongue and family and nation — humanity fragmented under judgment. Isaiah's promise gathers those same coastlands back under one law, and Pentecost reverses the tongues. The last places on the ancient map are exactly where the Servant's dominion is said to reach, which is why the missionary movement was reading these texts rightly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew i (H339), a habitable coastland, island — plural iyyim, the isles of the prophets; the word marks the outermost inhabited edge of the known world.

expand to see more

Hebrew i (H339) — coastland, island, region across the sea; the isles of the Gentiles (Gen 10:5) and the isles that wait for His law (Isa 42:4).

Hebrew iyyim — the plural; in Isaiah it functions as a synonym for the ends of the earth (Isa 41:5; Isa 49:1).

Greek nesos (G3520) — an island; the Septuagint's rendering, and the word for Patmos where the Revelation was given (Rev 1:9).

Usage

"“The isles shall wait for his law” — the Servant's reach measured at the map's edge."

"“The isles of the Gentiles divided… every one after his tongue” — Babel's scattering."

"“Let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” — the far coasts summoned to rejoice."
